questions.question: When is a function $f$ invertible?
questions.explanation: An inverse $Y\to X$ exists exactly when every $y\in Y$ comes from one and only one $x\in X$, which is bijectivity.

questions.question: If $f\colon X\to Y$ is a bijection, what is the domain of $f^{-1}$?
questions.explanation: Because $f$ maps $X$ onto $Y$, reversing its arrows makes $f^{-1}$ take inputs from $Y$ and output values in $X$.

$X\cap Y$ need not even equal either set and is not obtained by reversing the arrow.

questions.question: Which function is bijective on $\mathbb{R}$?
questions.explanation: The map $x\mapsto x^3$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$ and every real $y$ has the unique preimage $\sqrt[3]{y}$.

questions.question: What is the inverse of $f(x) = x^3$ on $\mathbb{R}$?

questions.question: Why does a bijection allow an inverse function to be defined?
options: Each $x\in X$ has exactly two images
Each $y\in Y$ has exactly one preimage $x\in X$
questions.explanation: Surjectivity supplies a preimage for each $y$, while injectivity makes that preimage unique; therefore reversing the assignment defines a function.

questions.question: If $f\colon X\to Y$ is injective but not surjective, what goes wrong with defining $f^{-1}$ on all of $Y$?
options: Some $y\in Y$ has too many preimages
Every $y\in Y$ has exactly one preimage
questions.explanation: Not surjective means $f(X)\ne Y$, so choose $y\in Y\setminus f(X)$; there is no $x$ with $f(x)=y$ and hence no value for $f^{-1}(y)$.

option_explanations: Injectivity rules out too many preimages; the actual failure is that at least one target has none.
Exactly one preimage for every $y$ would make $f$ both injective and surjective, contrary to the premise.
A nonempty domain is possible, for example $f\colon\{1\}\to\{a,b\}$ with $f(1)=a$.

questions.question: How can $f(x)=x^2$ be turned into a bijection?
options: It can never be made bijective
questions.explanation: On $[0,\infty)$, $x^2$ is strictly increasing and every $y\ge0$ has the unique preimage $\sqrt y$, so the restricted map is bijective.
questions.source_support: Bijective means both injective and surjective.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: On $\mathbb R$, $1$ and $-1$ still share the image $1$, while negative targets are never reached.
Changing the rule to $x^3$ creates a different function rather than making the stated square map bijective.
The restriction $[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is an explicit counterexample to 'never'.

questions.question: For a bijection $f\colon X\to Y$, what is $f^{-1}(f(x))$ for $x\in X$?
questions.explanation: Applying $f$ sends $x$ to its image, and applying $f^{-1}$ reverses that same assignment, so $f^{-1}(f(x))=x$.

$f(x)$ is the intermediate output before the inverse is applied.
The result is $0$ only for the particular input $x=0$, if $0\in X$.

questions.question: For a bijection $f$, what is $(f^{-1})^{-1}$?
questions.explanation: The inverse reverses every pair of $f$; reversing those pairs a second time restores $f$, hence $(f^{-1})^{-1}=f$.
questions.source_support: The inverse of a bijection is itself a bijection.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

Leaving it as $f^{-1}$ would reverse the pairs only once, not twice.
A bijection's inverse is itself bijective, so its inverse is defined.

questions.question: If a bijection exists between finite sets $X$ and $Y$, what must hold for their sizes?
questions.explanation: A bijection pairs every element of $X$ with exactly one distinct element of $Y$, exhausting both finite sets, so their cardinalities are equal.
questions.source_support: A bijection is a one-to-one correspondence.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: If $|X|>|Y|$, two elements of $X$ must share an image, contradicting injectivity.
If $|X|<|Y|$, at least one element of $Y$ is missed, contradicting surjectivity.
There is a strict size constraint for finite sets: a bijection requires equal cardinality.

questions.question: The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the graph of $f$ reflected across which line?
questions.explanation: Inversion swaps each point $(x,y)$ with $(y,x)$, which is exactly reflection in the line $y=x$.
questions.skill_detail: graph of the inverse is a reflection

option_explanations: Reflection in the $x$-axis maps $(x,y)$ to $(x,-y)$ and does not swap the coordinates.
Reflection in the $y$-axis maps $(x,y)$ to $(-x,y)$ rather than $(y,x)$.
Reflection in $y=-x$ maps $(x,y)$ to $(-y,-x)$, adding two sign changes.
